The last day of a path that winters over (Detroit, Chicago): the spec's 'by June 1837' for land bought in coin. A game choice, not a sourced date.

source: Blois, Gazetteer of the State of Michigan (1838), physical geography (r3 §2a)
note: Detroit navigation opens "from the 20th of March to the 1st of April". The game also ends the snow on the roads on this day; that use is the game's (r3 §7: no 1836-37 snow dates).
Chance of an event after a week wintering in a town (Detroit, Chicago); invented, the same as a day in town.
Chance of a day's hire in a winter town, below the autumn 0.7: r3 §7 has no Detroit winter wage series, only that labourers were wanted (Blois). Invented.

A room for the whole family by the night in a winter town. Invented: r3 §7 has no winter lodging series; the 50 cents is Kirkland's peak price for six feet of bar-room floor (one person), used here for a family's room.
From this date a family at Detroit is offered the winter there: the spec's 'after about 1 Nov'. Navigation closes about mid-December (r3 §2a, the researcher's estimate).

source: Silas Farmer, History of Detroit and Michigan (1884), the Panic of 1837 (r3 §2a)
note: The New York banks suspended on 10 May 1837; the news reached Detroit on 16 May, and the Detroit banks suspended on 17 May.
Michigan notes once the Detroit banks have suspended. Dove, Pecquet and Thies give 12.5 percent at Buffalo in November 1837 and later about 25; the Detroit spring rate itself is unsourced.
Illinois notes (Chicago wages and lot money on the Chicago path) once the Illinois banks have suspended (bank.suspend.illinois). Unsourced: taken at the game's Michigan figure, disc.miSuspended.

source: Blois, Gazetteer of the State of Michigan (1838), article White Pigeon (r3 §2b)
note: White Pigeon, on the Chicago road, is "144 [miles] from Detroit".

source: Blois, Gazetteer of the State of Michigan (1838), appendix p. 413 and article White Pigeon (r3 §2b)
note: Arithmetic on two printed figures: the Chicago road's whole length of 254 miles less White Pigeon's 144.
Days by stage from Detroit to Chicago. Blois prints the fare and 300 miles (r3 §2b) but no days; about 45 miles a day is invented.

source: Blois, Gazetteer of the State of Michigan (1838), appendix p. 415 (r3 §2b)
note: Cabin passage by water from Buffalo to Chicago, $20 ("$12 to Mackinac").

source: Blois, Gazetteer of the State of Michigan (1838), appendix p. 415 (r3 §2b)
note: Freight Buffalo to Chicago, 75 cents a hundredweight for heavy goods.
Days by steamboat from Buffalo round Mackinac to Chicago; Blois gives the fare but not the time. Invented.

What a town lot an emigrant family could reach cost in the autumn of 1836. Hoyt's lots ran from $100 (1830) to $100,000 (the best, 1836); r3 notes a family with $200 would buy on credit. The figure is invented.
The share paid down on a lot bought on credit; the rest is a note. Invented.

source: Hoyt, One Hundred Years of Land Values in Chicago (1933) (r3 §2b)
note: Interest rates in 1836 Chicago were "not less than 10 per cent per annum".
When a lot note falls due: a six-month term from the autumn, invented.
Market value of a lot on 15 September 1836 against the July peak. Hoyt: on 5 September the bids "fell short of the Commissioners' appraisals"; the 0.9 is invented.
How far lot values slide each week through the winter "lull" Hoyt describes; the rate is invented.

source: Hoyt, One Hundred Years of Land Values in Chicago (1933), pp. 39-40, Ogden to Butler, 17 June 1839 (r3 §2b)
note: "one 10th to a 20th is about all out town property will bring" (1839): the game takes the middle of that range from the bank suspension of 1837 on, earlier than Ogden's date.

source: Wikipedia, Chicago real estate bubble of the 1830s, summarizing Glaeser (2013) (r3 §2b)
note: Illinois banks suspended on 29 May 1837 (summary only).
Chance in a week that a buyer makes an offer for the family's lot through the autumn and winter. Invented.
Chance of a buyer in a week from the spring of 1837: few were buying. Ogden still sold at full prices that May (Hoyt), but he held the best property; invented.
The lowest offer, as a share of the lot's market value that week. Invented.
The highest offer, as a share of market value: in the mania some buyers still overpaid (Martineau via Hoyt). Invented.

source: Hoyt, One Hundred Years of Land Values in Chicago (1933) (r3 §2b)
